A canonical request carries correlation, messages, routing intent, required capabilities, sampling, output limits, streaming intent, tools, structured output and metadata, and is validated when it is built.
The message contract expresses the system, developer, user, assistant and tool roles independently of any provider's vocabulary.
The canonical response normalizes content, tool calls, finish reason, usage, latency, provider, model, endpoint, route and fallback chain, and the raw provider payload is never the public contract.
Tool definitions and tool calls are normalized into internal types with identifier, name and arguments, and the gateway executes no tool.
A tool call whose arguments are not valid JSON produces a normalized error instead of a partially parsed call.
Structured output is requested only from a model whose capability is known, and a request that needs it is refused or routed elsewhere rather than sent hopefully.
The contract carries an explicit version, so a consumer can detect an incompatible change instead of discovering one.
A provider contract declares health, model discovery, generation and streaming, and is not shaped by any one provider.
An OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions adapter builds the request, parses the response, parses the stream and maps the error.
An OpenAI-compatible Responses adapter builds the request, parses the response, parses the stream and maps the error.
An Anthropic-compatible Messages adapter builds the request, parses the response, parses the stream and maps the error.
The protocol is selected from the capabilities and endpoints the catalog records, the shape of the request and the provider configuration, never assumed from a default path.
A request that needs an endpoint the model does not declare is refused before it reaches the network.
No fictitious provider is registered in the runtime configuration; the deterministic double exists only inside the test fixtures.

Provider configuration is versionable and carries no credential value: an identifier, an adapter, an enabled flag, a base URL reference, the name of the secret variable, the discovery endpoint and the protocols supported.
The provider registry persists operational metadata — adapter, enabled state, health, last check and catalog state — and never a credential.
A credential is resolved from the environment at call time and reaches no database row, response body, log record, metric label or catalog record.
Every configuration key this Gate declares is read by the implementation.
A provider base URL is validated: HTTPS for a remote provider, plain HTTP only for a loopback address, and never user information embedded in the URL.
A provider address can never be supplied by an inference request; it comes from administrative configuration alone.
The catalog is discovered from the provider API, and no list written by hand is treated as authoritative.

A normalized model record carries the provider model identifier, display name, family, context window, maximum output tokens, supported endpoints, streaming, vision, tools, structured output, reasoning levels, active state, raw metadata and the synchronization instant.
An absent capability stays unknown and is never normalized into a negative answer.
Every capability records where it came from: provider metadata, manual configuration or observation, and never inference from a model's name.
Synchronization is idempotent: running it twice over the same provider answer changes nothing the second time.
A model that disappears from the provider answer is deactivated rather than destroyed, so the calls recorded against it stay readable.
A partial, invalid or failed synchronization leaves the previous catalog usable: the answer is validated and normalized before anything is committed.
Model identity is the provider together with the provider's own model identifier, so two providers exposing the same name do not collide.
Routing reads normalized fields; the raw provider metadata is kept for diagnosis and is never the thing a decision depends on.
The router is deterministic and applies a documented order: validate, explicit override, candidates, capability filter, context filter, route policy, configured priority, execution, fallback.
An explicit model is honored when the policy allows it and is refused, rather than silently replaced, when it cannot serve the request.
A default model is configurable, and a request with no model and no usable default fails with a clear error instead of an arbitrary choice.
Required capabilities eliminate candidates that cannot satisfy them, and an unknown capability is refused unless the policy explicitly allows it.
The gateway never knowingly sends a request larger than the context window it knows about, and an estimated token count is labelled an estimate rather than reported as exact.
A reasoning effort is validated against the levels the model or the provider declares, and an incompatible level produces a fallback or an explicit error rather than a silent send.
Route aliases are configuration, not built-in preference, and the system claims no empirical superiority for any of them.
No model quality score, benchmark result or comparative claim is invented anywhere in this Gate.
Every routing result carries a short structured explanation of the decision, and never a model's private reasoning.
A disabled provider and an inactive model are never selected.

An internal error taxonomy distinguishes authentication, authorization, rate limiting, unknown model, invalid request, context limit, provider unavailability, provider timeout, transient and permanent provider failure, an open circuit, cancellation and an internal gateway failure, and every adapter maps onto it.
Timeouts are configurable, connect and read are separated, and no provider call can hang without bound.
A retry happens only for an error class a retry can resolve, and never for authentication, authorization, an invalid request, an unknown model, an invalid schema or a context limit.
A provider's `Retry-After` is honored within a configured bound, and an unreasonably long wait is refused rather than obeyed.
Backoff is exponential with jitter, and the test suite controls time instead of waiting for it.
A circuit breaker moves between closed, open and half-open per provider and per provider and model, from external configuration.
The fallback chain is bounded, never repeats a candidate, cannot loop, and the chain that was used is recorded.
Fallback happens only for the error classes another candidate could resolve, and an invalid request is not retried against a second model.
A consumer that cancels interrupts the upstream call and the attempt is recorded as cancelled.
Request limits are configurable and enforced: payload size, message count, tool count, output tokens and fallback depth.
A provider response larger than the configured bound is refused instead of being read into memory without limit.
An unavailable provider never makes the Foundation liveness endpoint fail; it is visible in the gateway's own health instead.
Streaming goes through the same router and the same adapter abstraction as a non-streaming call, with no parallel architecture.
Stream events are normalized into an envelope covering start, text delta, tool-call delta, usage, end and error.
Automatic fallback is allowed only before the first content reaches the consumer; after it, the error is propagated and no second model continues the stream.
A stream that fails after content ends with an explicit error event carrying the partial result, not with a silent completion.
The API streams over Server-Sent Events and stops the upstream call when the client disconnects.
Usage is normalized where the provider supplies it — input, output, total, cached and reasoning tokens — and a field the provider did not supply stays absent rather than being invented.
Cost is absent unless pricing is configured, and zero is never used to mean unknown.
Every attempt is recorded with its operational metadata: correlation, provider, model, endpoint, route, status, timestamps, latency, tokens, error type, retries and fallbacks.
Prompts, messages and completions are not persisted by default; the debug capture is opt-in, redacted, documented and off in every shipped configuration.
A request fingerprint may be stored for correlation, and its documentation states that a hash is not anonymization.
No provider reasoning content is stored; only the reasoning token count a provider reports.
Nothing this Gate persists becomes training data: the rights defaults of the provenance policy are preserved.
The gateway exposes request, duration, error, retry, fallback, circuit state, provider health and catalog size metrics through the existing Prometheus endpoint.

The run lifecycle is an explicit state machine over exactly the declared states, and no state exists that the contract does not name.
A transition happens only when the transition table allows it.
An impossible transition is refused with a typed error rather than silently applied.
A terminal state is terminal: no transition leaves `SUCCEEDED`, `FAILED` or `CANCELLED`.
Re-running a task creates a new run; a terminal run is never resumed in place.
Every accepted state change records an event, so the history explains the state.
The state machine is one definition, used by the API, the workflow and the store alike.
The event vocabulary covers run creation and start, agent start and completion, model call start and completion, tool request and tool result, and the three terminal outcomes.
Events of one run carry a monotonic sequence number assigned by the store, so their order is deterministic.
A recorded event is never rewritten; a correction is a new event.
A retried append does not create a second event for the same occurrence.
An event payload carries a short verifiable summary and never a model's private reasoning or a raw prompt.
An event payload larger than the configured bound is refused rather than persisted.
An agent profile is a versioned contract carrying identity, role, description, prompt template, default route, turn limit, permitted actions and an enabled flag.
The builtin profiles are exactly the four this Gate needs to prove the runtime, and no profile exists for a capability the Gate does not exercise.
Profiles are loaded from the repository, enumerable through the runtime, and validated when they are loaded.
Loading the builtin profiles is idempotent: running it twice changes nothing the second time.
Prompt templates are versioned files under the agent definition directory, not strings concatenated across the code.
An agent run records the profile version and the prompt template hash that produced it, so its behaviour can be reproduced.
Prompt assembly keeps runtime instructions, role instructions, task content and tool results in separate labelled channels.
The user's task is carried in the user channel and is never concatenated into the system instructions.
Every executed step records run, task, agent, agent run, timestamps, model call identity, provider, model, template version and result status — and no private reasoning.
A profile declares the actions it may request, and a tool request outside that set is refused instead of persisted.
A team profile is a versioned, ordered list of stages, each naming an agent profile, its input mapping and the name of its output.
Two builtin teams exist: one single-agent and one two-stage planner and reviewer.
Team composition is configuration. Nothing in this Gate invents a team, and no model decides which agents run.
Stages execute in the order the profile declares, and each stage's output becomes explicit, named context for the next.
A previous stage's output reaches the next stage as a labelled artifact and never as an instruction.
A team run produces one agent run per stage, in order, with separate outputs.
A turn produces exactly one of a final answer, a message or a tool request.
The envelope carries an explicit version and is documented, so a consumer can detect an incompatible change instead of discovering one.
The parser is strict: an output that does not conform is rejected rather than partially accepted.
Native structured output is requested only from a model whose capability is known; otherwise the envelope is validated JSON text produced by the same contract.
No capability is asserted on a model's behalf to make a turn work.
At most one repair attempt follows an invalid turn, and it happens through the Model Gateway like any other call.
A repair call counts against the run's budget and is recorded as a repair rather than hidden.
A second invalid output ends the run with a normalised invalid-output error rather than looping.
Every inference this Gate performs travels through the Model Gateway client port and through nothing else.
A run may carry a route alias or an explicit model, and the gateway decides whether it can be served.
A run that names neither uses the configured default, and the runtime never picks a provider itself.
Every model call is attributed to the agent run that caused it.
A definitive gateway failure ends the run with a normalised error; the run never stays `RUNNING` for ever.
The runtime does not repeat a whole model call the gateway has already exhausted its own retries on.
Cost the gateway does not know is reported as unknown and never as zero.
A request the model's context cannot hold produces an explicit error rather than a silent truncation of the task.

requirements.section: 10. Tool requests and the Gate 3 boundary
requirements.description: A tool request is a persisted contract carrying identity, run, agent, name, arguments, creation time and a status from the declared vocabulary.

requirements.section: 10. Tool requests and the Gate 3 boundary
requirements.description: A tool result is a contract carrying the request it answers, a status, an output, an error and metadata.

requirements.section: 10. Tool requests and the Gate 3 boundary
requirements.description: A tool request turn persists the request, records the event and moves the run to `WAITING_FOR_TOOL`.

requirements.section: 10. Tool requests and the Gate 3 boundary
requirements.description: A paused run performs no further model call until a result arrives.

requirements.section: 10. Tool requests and the Gate 3 boundary
requirements.description: A tool name is data. Nothing in this Gate interprets it as a command, a path or an executable.

requirements.section: 10. Tool requests and the Gate 3 boundary
requirements.description: A matching tool result is persisted, recorded as an event and resumes the run.

requirements.section: 10. Tool requests and the Gate 3 boundary
requirements.description: The same tool result delivered twice resolves the request once and resumes the run once.

requirements.section: 10. Tool requests and the Gate 3 boundary
requirements.description: A tool result naming another run or an unknown request is refused.

requirements.section: 10. Tool requests and the Gate 3 boundary
requirements.description: A tool result that arrives after the run reached a terminal state is refused.

requirements.section: 10. Tool requests and the Gate 3 boundary
requirements.description: Waiting for a tool has its own configurable timeout, separate from the run deadline, and reaching it ends the run explicitly.

requirements.section: 10. Tool requests and the Gate 3 boundary
requirements.description: An automated control proves the runtime boundary contains no process, shell, filesystem-mutating or version-control execution path, and the control is a property of the boundary rather than of one file.

requirements.section: 10. Tool requests and the Gate 3 boundary
requirements.description: The division of labour with the next Gate is documented: this Gate persists and pauses, the next one executes.
Every run carries a maximum turn count, a maximum model-call count and a wall-clock deadline.
A token budget is enforced when the provider reports usage and recorded as unenforceable when it does not, rather than invented.
A budget that is zero, negative or absurd is refused when the run is validated.
Reaching any budget ends the run with a normalised budget error.
No model call happens after a budget is exhausted.
Every call to the gateway counts against the model-call budget, including a repair.
A run cannot execute an unbounded number of turns, and a run that outlives its deadline is ended rather than left running.
A run can be cancelled through the API while it is executing.
Cancellation reaches the durable workflow and stops it rather than only marking a row.
A cancelled run is terminal and records the cancellation event.
A run waiting for a tool can be cancelled, and a tool result that arrives afterwards is refused.
No model call happens after a run is cancelled.
Temporal is the durable execution engine, and no second scheduler or background orchestration loop competes with it.
Workflow code stays deterministic: every external effect — model call, persistence, notification — happens in an activity.
A worker restart while a run waits for a tool preserves the run, and the run resumes and completes when the result arrives.
An API restart does not lose a run in progress: the state lives in the store and in the workflow, never in process memory.
The workflow receives a frozen plan, so editing a profile while a run executes cannot change what that run is doing.

requirements.section: 14. The HTTP API and the event stream
requirements.description: A versioned API creates a run, reads it, lists runs, streams its events, cancels it and accepts a tool result.

requirements.section: 14. The HTTP API and the event stream
requirements.description: Creation answers immediately with the run identifier, its state and its creation time, without holding the request open for the run.

requirements.section: 14. The HTTP API and the event stream
requirements.description: Creation accepts no provider credential and no provider address.

requirements.section: 14. The HTTP API and the event stream
requirements.description: A run's status carries its state, current stage, timestamps, budget consumption, final result when there is one and error summary when there is one.

requirements.section: 14. The HTTP API and the event stream
requirements.description: A failed run answers with an error type, a safe message, the stage that failed and the correlation identifier, and never with a traceback.

requirements.section: 14. The HTTP API and the event stream
requirements.description: Run events are readable as a page and as a live stream.

requirements.section: 14. The HTTP API and the event stream
requirements.description: A consumer that reconnects with a cursor receives exactly the events that follow it.

requirements.section: 14. The HTTP API and the event stream
requirements.description: Reconnecting or retrying a read creates no new event.

requirements.section: 14. The HTTP API and the event stream
requirements.description: The available agent profiles and team profiles are enumerable through the API.

requirements.section: 14. The HTTP API and the event stream
requirements.description: Task input size is bounded by configuration and an oversized task is refused rather than stored.
A creation request repeated with the same idempotency key returns the run the first one created.
A creation request with a different key creates a different run.
Two runs execute at the same time without sharing state, context or events.
One task may carry two independent runs with separate results and separate events.
Identifiers use the strategy the repository already defines rather than a second format.
The runtime publishes the declared instruments for runs, turns, failures, waiting runs, budget exhaustions and cancellations.
No metric label carries a task, a prompt, a response or tool arguments, and every label is low cardinality.
Structured logs carry correlation, task, run, agent, agent run, stage, event type, model call and status when those exist.
No log record carries the whole task by default, and a secret nested inside a payload is redacted.
An operational page creates a run from a written task, a chosen team and an optional route or model.
The page follows the run's state and its events as they happen.
The page shows the final result of a successful run and the safe failure summary of a failed one.
The page can cancel a run that is executing.
A run waiting for a tool is shown as waiting, with the tool name and the pending status, and the page offers nothing that would execute it.
Model output is rendered as text, never as trusted markup.
No provider credential reaches the runtime, the store, a log record, a metric or the browser.
Tool arguments, agent output and tool results are bounded by configuration, and an oversized payload is refused.
Nothing this Gate persists becomes training data: rights default to denial and no run, event or result is marked otherwise.
The runtime asks for no private reasoning and stores none; what it keeps are short verifiable summaries.
A single-agent run executes live, through the Model Gateway, against the configured provider, and succeeds.
A planner and reviewer run executes live, in order, with separate outputs and the reviewer receiving the planner's output.
The live check uses an explicitly configured model and fails clearly when that model is not in the catalog, rather than substituting one.
The live check reports `BLOCKED` rather than `FAIL` when the local configuration carries no credential, and names the variable that is missing.
The live evidence records model provenance — provider, model, endpoint, model call identity — and no prompt or completion.
The repository's one verification command covers this Gate, in its targeted and its full mode.
A runbook documents starting the runtime, creating a run, following it, cancelling it, tool requests and results, budgets, the live smoke and troubleshooting.
The architecture, development, version and entry documents describe what this Gate delivered rather than what was planned.
The structural decisions of this Gate are recorded as ADRs.
The Gate produces its retrospective from the canonical template.

requirements.description: The Gate closes at the project's own internal verdict and starts no part of the Gate that follows it.
A canonical, machine-readable requirement specification exists for this Gate and the registry mirrors it row for row.
The closed mandatory gate registry carries the executable gate this Gate introduces, and that gate builds what it measures before measuring it.
requirements.evidence: A Green Keeper cycle measured against the registry's mandatory set; `Gate3MandatoryGateTests`.

requirements.description: The test suite this Gate introduces is declared canonically, is counted by the count derivation and is resolvable as evidence.
The internal Red Team battery of this Gate is executable, scoped to the sandbox, runs its attacks against the real container engine and records a null-mutation control.
The reservation of the sandbox directory is consumed by the Gate that owns it, and every reservation of a later Gate is still enforced.
One documented command verifies this Gate, adds the stages it introduces and keeps a targeted mode that does not restart the stack.
The repository publishes to exactly one authorised remote, and a remote pointing anywhere else is refused rather than used.
The whole history was scanned for credentials before its first publication, and a finding names the commit, the file, the line and the kind but never the value.
The published history carries no credential, and the check is repeatable against the history as it now stands.
Every push is preceded by a scan of exactly the staged content, and an allowance matches a value's digest rather than a path.
Whether the branch and the checkpoint tag are on the remote is asked of the remote, an unpushed commit or a missing tag fails, and an unreachable remote is never a pass.

The commit, push, tag and correction rules are stated in the development contract and recorded as a decision: atomic commits, green commits only, no rewriting of published history, no moving of a published tag, and no credential in a URL, a configuration or a versioned file.
The history of this Gate's development is preserved as observable data — requirement, commits, tests, fixes, checkpoint — and nothing in it is marked as training-eligible.

requirements.section: 3. Defects inherited from the previous Gate
requirements.description: A command the ledger could not replay is refused before it executes, the refusal is itself recorded, and the recorder and the validator apply one shared replayability rule.

requirements.section: 3. Defects inherited from the previous Gate
requirements.description: A guardrail entry that names a file or a path where a test is required is refused, and lesson validation and guardrail effectiveness resolve an entry through one function.

requirements.section: 3. Defects inherited from the previous Gate
requirements.description: The committed lesson index is the render of the memory, and a memory changed without re-rendering it, or an index edited by hand, is refused under the memory policy that introduced the rule.

requirements.section: 3. Defects inherited from the previous Gate
requirements.description: The event stream of a run that is already terminal delivers every event after the cursor, however many pages that takes, before it closes.

requirements.section: 3. Defects inherited from the previous Gate
requirements.description: A canonical ADR index exists, lists every record with its title and status, resolves every link, and its test asserts rather than skips.
The sandbox is its own service in the directory the scope registry reserved for it, with its own contracts, and the decision is recorded.
No sandbox logic lives in the API routes, the Agent Runtime or the Model Gateway: none of them imports the sandbox package or a container client.
The Agent Runtime and the workflow that drives it still execute nothing themselves; a tool reaches the sandbox only as an activity on the sandbox's own task queue.
Inside the sandbox service only the engine backend and the in-container helper start a process, and the controller never uses a shell.
The controller starts only the container client, with an argument vector, and never a command a request supplied.
The controller is the only service given the container engine, and it holds no capability, cannot gain one, and publishes no port.

Versioned contracts exist for the sandbox session, the policy, the workspace, the execution request, the execution result, the command execution, the file operation, the Git operation and the artifact reference.
A contract of another version is refused rather than interpreted, and a request carrying a field the contract does not declare or missing one it requires is refused.

A command result carries the exit code, standard output, standard error, duration, whether it timed out, whether it was truncated and its artifact references, and no exit code is invented for a command that never started.
The execution status, session state, workspace and operation vocabularies are closed, and the database accepts exactly the declared ones.
The result an agent receives cannot present a cancellation, a denial or a timeout as a success.

requirements.section: 6. The tool registry and the tool policy
requirements.description: An explicit registry names every executable tool — list, read, write, patch and search of files, shell execution, and the local Git status, diff, log, show, add and commit — and only a registered name can execute.

requirements.section: 6. The tool registry and the tool policy
requirements.description: An unknown tool name is refused, and no name is ever mapped to a shell.

requirements.section: 6. The tool registry and the tool policy
requirements.description: A canonical sandbox tool policy defines, per policy, the allowed tools, the resource profile, the network profile, the workspace permissions, the command timeout and the output limits.

requirements.section: 6. The tool registry and the tool policy
requirements.description: A tool the run's policy does not allow is refused, a policy naming an unregistered tool is refused, and an unknown policy is refused.

requirements.section: 6. The tool registry and the tool policy
requirements.description: Tool arguments are structured and typed: an undeclared argument is refused, and a wrong type, an absent value and a wrong value each carry their own reason.

requirements.section: 6. The tool registry and the tool policy
requirements.description: No request can change its policy, its limits, its network or its mounts; a request that tries is denied, and a request may lower a timeout but never raise it.

requirements.section: 6. The tool registry and the tool policy
requirements.description: The limits a tool runs under come from the policy, and every limit a policy applies is inside its declared bound.

requirements.section: 6. The tool registry and the tool policy
requirements.description: A policy document with an unknown key, or a read-only policy that allows a writing tool, is refused when it is loaded.

requirements.section: 6. The tool registry and the tool policy
requirements.description: Tools the policy allows execute automatically, inside the sandbox, without a confirmation per call; nothing is executed on the host under any policy.
Every run executes in its own disposable container with its own workspace; two runs never share either.
The sandbox runs unprivileged, as a non-root user, with every capability dropped and no way to gain privileges.
The root filesystem is read-only, and the only writable places are the workspace and a temporary directory, both in-memory filesystems with a size limit.
The container engine's socket, and any other engine endpoint, is absent from a sandbox.
No host path is mounted into a sandbox — no drive, no root, no home, no profile, no SSH directory, no credential store, no secret environment file — and no argument of a request can add one.
Every sandbox container carries labels naming the service instance that owns it, the session, the run, the policy and its expiry, so ownership is read from the engine rather than from memory.
CPU, memory, process count, workspace size, execution timeout and output size are mandatory, configurable limits, and a zero, negative, absurd or missing value is refused.
The memory limit holds the in-memory filesystems, so a full workspace cannot starve the processes of the limit they were promised.
A process that multiplies without end is contained by the process limit, and the sandbox remains usable afterwards.
A process that exceeds the memory limit fails in a controlled way, and the host is unaffected.
The workspace cannot outgrow its limit.
A command that exceeds its timeout is ended together with every process it started, including a process that left its session, and nothing is left running.
Standard output and standard error are bounded while they are read; what exceeds the bound is truncated explicitly and stored whole as an artifact, and memory is never unbounded.
A sandbox has no network by default: only loopback exists, and every policy the Gate ships denies the network.
An attempt to reach an external address from a sandbox without network fails.
The one other network profile is local services only, on an internal network with no route outside, and it is chosen by the policy, never by a request.
No package installation from the internet is offered; the image carries the toolchain the Gate's tests need.
A sandbox receives only the variables its policy explicitly allows, and no variable of the controller — provider key, repository token, agent socket, cloud credential or engine address — reaches it.
A command's environment inside the sandbox is the allowlist and nothing else.
A policy cannot allow a credential-shaped variable into a command's environment.
No Git credential, credential helper, SSH key or agent socket exists in a sandbox.
A workspace has an identity and an explicit lifecycle, belongs to exactly one run, and a run holds at most one active session.
A workspace is provisioned only from an authorised snapshot, named by its artifact identifier and never by a path, and becomes a repository the tools can work on.
Anything but a workspace snapshot artifact is refused before the run exists, and a snapshot for a team that executes no tool is refused.
A snapshot whose digest differs from its record, or that carries a link or an escaping member, is refused, and no session survives the refusal.
One run cannot read or write another run's files, nor see its processes.
The development working tree of this repository is never an agent's workspace.

requirements.section: 12. The path resolver and the filesystem tools
requirements.description: One canonical path resolver decides every path a tool touches; no other module re-implements path safety.

requirements.section: 12. The path resolver and the filesystem tools
requirements.description: Traversal, absolute paths, drive letters, UNC paths, null bytes and normalisation tricks are refused, each with its own reason.

requirements.section: 12. The path resolver and the filesystem tools
requirements.description: A link inside the workspace that points outside it cannot be read or written through, whether it names a file, a directory, the root or climbs out relatively; a link that stays inside is followed.

requirements.section: 12. The path resolver and the filesystem tools
requirements.description: Listing, reading, writing, searching and patching work inside the workspace of a real sandbox.

requirements.section: 12. The path resolver and the filesystem tools
requirements.description: A read and a write are bounded in size, an oversized one is refused, and binary content is refused as text rather than mangled.

requirements.section: 12. The path resolver and the filesystem tools
requirements.description: A write validates its parent directory and replaces the file atomically.

requirements.section: 12. The path resolver and the filesystem tools
requirements.description: A patch applies only inside the workspace; a patch whose context does not match, or that has one bad file, changes nothing.

requirements.section: 12. The path resolver and the filesystem tools
requirements.description: A search is confined to the workspace and bounded in results, output and duration.

requirements.section: 12. The path resolver and the filesystem tools
requirements.description: A path refused inside the sandbox reaches the agent as a denial, not as a failure of the sandbox.
Shell execution runs only inside the sandbox container, with the command, the working directory, the allowed environment and the timeout passed as structured arguments.
Standard output, standard error, a zero and a non-zero exit code, a missing executable and a child process are all reported faithfully.
The working directory resolves inside the workspace, and an escaping one is refused.
A payload that tries to reach a host command affects only the sandbox, inside its policy, and the host is unchanged.
A command still running when its run is cancelled is stopped, with every process it started.
Inside the workspace an agent can read the status, the working and the staged diff, the log and a commit, stage files and commit locally.
Every Git tool builds a fixed argument vector, a revision that looks like an option is refused, and a commit skips hooks and carries its message as one argument.
No remote Git operation is offered or possible — no push, fetch, clone or remote — and no destructive operation — hard reset, clean, rebase, history filtering, forced push — is offered by default.
An agent's commits carry an explicit sandbox identity that is not a person, separate from the owner's development identity, and the difference is documented.
Git output is bounded like any other output.
A session moves through explicit states, is created ready for its run and is removed with it.
A running tool holds its session in the running state, and inspecting a session reports the store and the engine side by side.
When a run ends or is cancelled its sandbox is removed, and no container or temporary volume is left behind.
A restarted service reconciles from the store and the engine rather than from memory: it keeps a live session, removes a container no session owns, and fails a session whose container vanished.
Reconciliation touches only containers this service instance owns, so another stack or a test on the same engine is never cleaned up by it.
An orphan sweeper expires only sessions that have expired and are not running, in bounded, deterministic batches, and never removes an active workspace.
This Gate adds its schema through a new migration and edits no migration that has already been applied.
The existing tool call, artifact and run entities are evolved rather than duplicated, and the one new table holds only what nothing else could: the sandbox session.
A database created from nothing reaches the head revision, and a database at the previous Gate's head upgrades without losing a row.
Every execution is traceable from the task through the run, the agent run, the tool request, the sandbox session and the execution to the result, and none of it holds private reasoning.
A retried request never executes twice: the execution is keyed by the tool request it answers.
The store the service runs against in the stack records sessions and executions in the real database with the same behaviour the suite asserts in memory.
Nothing this Gate persists is training-eligible, and no table stores a credential.
A pending tool request of a stage with a sandbox policy is checked against the policy, executed in the run's sandbox, its result persisted, and the workflow resumes.
A stage without a sandbox policy keeps the previous Gate's behaviour: the request waits for a result delivered through the API.
The run plan names the sandbox policy of each stage and the workspace source, frozen when the run is created.
A tool result returns to the agent as labelled data in its own channel and never as an instruction.
A large result reaches the model truncated inline with an artifact reference, within the size the runtime accepts for a tool result.
A tool that times out returns a normalised error result the agent receives, and the run never stays waiting for a tool for ever.
Cancelling a run during a long command stops the command, records the cancellation, ends the run cancelled and leaves no process behind.
A sandbox service restart while a run executes does not lose the run: the session is reconciled and the run completes.

requirements.section: 18. Agent profiles and the coding team
requirements.description: A profile that may request tools names the sandbox policy that governs them, and a profile with tools and no policy is refused.

requirements.section: 18. Agent profiles and the coding team
requirements.description: No agent is given every tool: each profile's permitted actions are within its policy's tools.

requirements.section: 18. Agent profiles and the coding team
requirements.description: A developer profile may read, search, write, patch, run tests and use the local Git tools its policy allows.

requirements.section: 18. Agent profiles and the coding team
requirements.description: The reviewer is read-only: read, search, diff and test results, and no writing tool.

requirements.section: 18. Agent profiles and the coding team
requirements.description: The planner has no writing tool and works from context alone.

requirements.section: 18. Agent profiles and the coding team
requirements.description: A minimal coding team — planner, developer, reviewer — proves the flow, and no larger team is built.
Full output, large diffs and workspace snapshots are stored in the existing artifact infrastructure, recorded as artifacts, and no second store is created.
A workspace snapshot is created from an explicit source directory by a documented command, and never from the development working tree implicitly.
A registry of sandbox image profiles exists, the architecture accepts new profiles, and one functional profile for this project carries Git and Python.
The image is built as part of the Gate from a base pinned by digest and packages pinned by version, and never from a moving tag.
The image is addressed by a fingerprint of its inputs, and a missing or stale image is refused rather than substituted.
The sandbox gate builds the service image and the sandbox image before it measures anything.

The sandbox service installs the one dependency lock the dependency scan reads, so its Python dependencies are scanned with the rest; the sandbox image's system packages are pinned by version, and what the scan does not cover is documented rather than implied.
An internal service contract creates a session, executes a tool, inspects a session and terminates it, and it is reached only as activities on the sandbox's task queue.
A refusal is recorded as an execution with its reason, so a denied request is as traceable as an executed one.
The service's health is a poller on its queue and an engine that answers, not a process that exists.
The service publishes instruments for sessions created and active, tool executions, their duration, failures, timeouts and policy refusals.
Every metric label is low cardinality, a command never becomes a label, and a refusal is counted by its reason.
Logs carry the run, the agent, the sandbox, the tool, the status and the duration, and never a whole result, a secret or the host environment.
The observability stack scrapes the sandbox service.
The run page shows each tool the sandbox executed: the tool, its status, its duration, the abbreviated sandbox identifier and a summary.
The page never receives a tool's output and offers no interactive shell.
The command line interface stays reserved for the Gate that owns it.

A synthetic repository with a defective function and a failing test is provisioned as a snapshot, and a coding run over it reads the code, runs the failing test, patches the code, runs the passing test, reads the diff, commits locally, is reviewed and finishes.
The scenario drives the real workflow, the real activities, the real sandbox service and the real container engine, with only the model replaced by a deterministic script.
An automatic proof shows a shell request did not execute on the host: a sentinel outside the sandbox is neither created nor modified.
The scenario asserts what the run recorded — its terminal state, its tool executions and the test that passed — rather than what the harness sent.
The repository's one verification command covers this Gate, in its targeted and its full mode.
A runbook documents the lifecycle, the tool policy, the filesystem, the shell, Git, the network, resources, artifacts, cleanup, debugging and the security boundary.
The architecture, development, version and entry documents describe what this Gate delivered rather than what was planned.
The structural decisions of this Gate are recorded as ADRs and listed in the index.
The Gate produces its retrospective from the canonical template, and its reusable lessons are recorded with the guardrail that protects the property rather than one file.
